name: Coaching and Evaluation
title: Coaching and Evaluation
answer: Coaching and evaluation is the idea that AI can help instructional coaches and principals turn observation notes into clearer coaching conversations, while AI analysis of classroom video stays out of teacher evaluation. It matters because coaching feedback is where teacher growth happens, and because the book reports that AI models rating classroom videos were not consistent enough to affect a teacher's job. Walkthrough trends can support schoolwide professional learning only when they are kept separate from judging individual teachers.

sections.body: Instructional coaches and principals observe teachers and give feedback, and AI can help them organize observation notes into clear, useful coaching conversations. A coach might use an approved tool to draft a summary of strengths and next steps from their notes, then revise it before meeting the teacher. The conversation between coach and teacher is where growth happens. The idea addresses the need to turn observation notes into productive coaching conversations while keeping the human conversation central. It also draws a line: AI analysis of classroom video should stay out of teacher evaluation, and walkthrough trends should be kept separate from evaluation.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, a coach or principal can use an approved AI tool to draft a summary of strengths and next steps from their observation notes, then revise that draft before meeting the teacher. The meeting itself remains a conversation between coach and teacher, because that is where growth happens. A principal might also use AI to summarize patterns across many brief classroom visits, such as how often students discuss ideas with each other. Those trends can guide schoolwide professional learning without judging individual teachers. Teachers should know how walkthrough data is used.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book's evidence for this idea is a study of eight AI models rating classroom videos, which found that their agreement with certified human observers was moderate at best, and their ratings changed from one run to the next (Melo et al., 2026). The same text states that the models relied on what was said aloud and missed much of the context that trained observers see. The book uses this finding to argue that tools this inconsistent should not affect a teacher's job. No other study, figure, or finding is given for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text: AI analysis of classroom video should stay out of teacher evaluation, and tools that are inconsistent should not affect a teacher's job. Walkthrough trends can be useful only when they are kept separate from evaluation and do not judge individual teachers. Teachers should know how walkthrough data is used. The decisions that stay with people include revising the AI draft before a coaching meeting and holding the coaching conversation itself, because that conversation is where growth happens. The principal also decides how walkthrough trends guide schoolwide professional learning rather than individual evaluation.
